summary: Follow-up to the 2025-02-28 production incident where serving latency and partial degradation affected Acme Health's inference pipelines. Discussed immediate mitigations (circuit breaker, KV cache patch, autoscaler tuning), short-term reliability improvements, obligations (security docs, credits), and next steps for remediation and testing.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-03-05
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Smith (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SRE), Tina Alvarez (CSM) -- Maria Gonzalez (Acme Eng Manager), Samir Khan (Acme SRE), Lena Wu (Acme Head of Product), Ethan Park (Acme Security), Olivia Reed (Acme Support)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Follow-up on incident, agree on root cause (KV cache invalidation + autoscaler mis-trigger), patch timeline, runbook updates, compensation and SLAs; schedule for canary/fallback testing.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Okay hi everyone thanks for jumping on, we wanted to follow up on the postmortem and make sure the mitigations we proposed are clear and that we have owners.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Maria): Thanks Jordan, appreciate it. I just want to make sure the credentialing and audit bits are good for our compliance team, they asked about SOC two and SAML, right, SOC two, S O C 2?
00:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Yes SOC 2, we updated the security packet and I emailed Ethan last night with the SOCII - uh sorry, SOC 2 evidence links and the SAML SSO config doc.
00:45 Speaker 3 (Priya): Quick agenda: recap root cause, short-term mitigations we rolled out during the incident, longer-term reliability changes, then action items.
00:58 Speaker 4 (Samir): Recap from our side: during the incident we saw a KV cache invalidation cascading with a flapping autoscaler, a lot of cold-starts for Dedicated pool nodes and a backlog of queued requests. Latency spiked and the fallback model wasn't triggered fast enough.
01:22 Speaker 3 (Priya): Right, and to add, some of the logs show that the KV cache eviction happened around 03:12 UTC and there was an unexpected memory pressure signal that GC'd shard data. The runtime ended up thrashing, our prefix cache misses spiked from 4% to 62% which made the kernel selections go into a slower path.
01:48 Speaker 5 (Marcus): There was also a mis-configuration in the cluster autoscaler that preferred scale-up into a single rack which hit a hotspot on PCI bus; so provisioning latency was higher than our usual median.
02:05 Speaker 2 (Maria): We'd like to understand why the fallback model switch didn't happen. Can you explain the policy?
02:15 Speaker 3 (Priya): The fallback is policy-driven by latency and error thresholds. During the incident the error ratio crossed threshold but because the autoscaler kept retrying to provision higher-capacity nodes, the policy oscillated. Essentially the system expected capacity soon but it never met the health probes so the circuit breaker didn't trip.
02:34 Speaker 4 (Samir): So the circuit-breaker gating was too permissive. We need a faster failover, ideally model variants with lower memory footprints, and an immediate circuit-breaker override option.
02:50 Speaker 3 (Priya): Agreed. Short-term mitigations we put in place: manual circuit-breaker toggle for Acme Dedicated pools, temporary increase in warm instances to avoid cold starts, and an emergency KV cache patch which reduces memory churn by changing eviction policy. We also rolled throttling at the router to shed non-critical requests.
03:14 Speaker 6 (Lena): From product perspective it's crucial we have deterministic behavior during incidents — our workflows time out and that causes user-visible failures.
03:28 Speaker 3 (Priya): Understood. On the patch side, the KV cache change is a hotfix that we validated on staging, it reduces the worst case by about 40% in our bench runs. We'll push to canary tomorrow, then to alpha for Acme, then to prod in a controlled window.
03:46 Speaker 5 (Marcus): For autoscaler tuning, proposed changes are: reduce the scale-up aggregation window, add cross-rack distribution preference, and pre-warm a small standby pool for critical customers. That should reduce provisioning tail latency.
04:10 Speaker 2 (Maria): About compensations — Olivia, did you already propose credits?
04:18 Speaker 7 (Olivia): Yes, support suggested a service credit for the incident period; Tina will follow up with a specific credit amount and contract notes.
04:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): I'll include the official postmortem doc and the RCA links in the email after this call. The doc has timeline, logs links, and the mitigation rollout plan: https://redwood.internal/postmortem/acme-20250228 (internal link).
04:48 Speaker 4 (Samir): On monitoring: our alerts were noisy but didn't capture the KV cache eviction pattern early. Can we add a dedicated metric for prefix-cache hit rate and a low-latency warning?
05:02 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes, we can emit prefix_cache_hit_ratio and a derived alert if hit ratio drops below 85% for 3 consecutive minutes. We'll also push traces to their tracing backend — we saw sampling was too low during the spike.
05:24 Speaker 6 (Lena): Also need clearer runbooks. During the incident there was confusion about who triggers the circuit-breaker and who authorizes node restarts.
05:38 Speaker 5 (Marcus): We'll update the runbook: explicit owner (Redwood SRE) for circuit-breaker, on-call contact for Acme SRE, and step-by-step steps including when to escalate to Eng. We'll attach command snippets.
05:55 Speaker 2 (Maria): For the medium-term changes, what's the timeline?
06:03 Speaker 3 (Priya): Short-term (1 week): KV cache hotfix to canary and config change for circuit-breaker settings. Medium (3-6 weeks): autoscaler guardrails, standby pool, runbook updates, and canary testing. Long-term (quarter): improve kernel selection heuristics and model variant rollout automation.
06:26 Speaker 4 (Samir): On security/compliance — Ethan here, we need any changes to logging or retention for audits. Did the incident require any data egress review?
06:38 Speaker 8 (Ethan): We looked through audit logs; no user data left the environment, but we'd like confirmation on KMS rotations and that logs are retained for 365 days for our internal policy.
06:52 Speaker 1 (Jordan): We will confirm KMS rotation schedule and log retention policy — I sent the security packet already, but we'll add the specific retention confirmation.
07:05 Speaker 6 (Lena): On the fallback models: can you publish a list of compatible low-memory variants we can expect for our workloads? Some of our prompts are long and we rely on higher context, so fallback has to be careful.
07:20 Speaker 3 (Priya): We'll share a compatibility matrix and suggested prompt truncation policies. We'll also show quantization options and estimated quality delta for typical Acme prompts.
07:36 Speaker 2 (Maria): During the incident we also saw higher costs due to repeated retries; any idea how to avoid cost spikes?
07:46 Speaker 5 (Marcus): Throttling non-critical routes and better retry/backoff policies help; also circuit-breaker plus standby pool so you don't spin up large capacity repeatedly. We'll include cost monitoring and token-level cost breakdowns in the dashboard for Acme.
08:05 Speaker 7 (Olivia): Support log: we captured all customer tickets and internal comms, attached to the postmortem.
08:12 Speaker 3 (Priya): A couple of technical notes for the record:
- Our runtime's kernel selection fell back to a generic attention kernel under memory pressure; we should prioritize an alternative low-memory kernel for the long-tail sequences.
- The KV cache eviction algorithm we shipped was LRU with a subtle bug in multi-shard coordination that produced excessive evictions under bursty writes.
- The autoscaler used a single-metric policy (CPU) instead of a composite score (CPU + queue length + cache miss ratio) which made decisions noisier.

08:48 Speaker 4 (Samir): Good catch on composite autoscaler metrics. Can Redwood share the proposed composite formula so we can run a dry-run in our staging?
08:58 Speaker 3 (Priya): Yes we'll share the tuning doc and a simulation tool we use internally. We'll also provide a script to replay the incident profile against their staging cluster.
09:12 Speaker 6 (Lena): About testing — can we run a canary with 10% of traffic and synthetic load that mimics our production prompt mixes?
09:21 Speaker 3 (Priya): Absolutely. Plan is: canary + synthetic replay + smoke asserts for latency and quality. We'll coordinate on traffic split and rollback criteria.
09:35 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Action recap — Jordan will share postmortem and compensation; Priya will run repro and share patches; Marcus will propose autoscaler and standby pool config; Samir will validate alerts; Tina/Olivia will coordinate credits. We'll set the follow-up in two weeks.
09:58 Speaker 4 (Samir): One last ask — is there a way to get a passive read-only view into Redwood's observability for our SREs? The more context they have the faster they can react.
10:10 Speaker 1 (Jordan): We can set up a read-only dashboard link and short-lived creds for their oncall; I noted that as an action.
10:20 Speaker 6 (Lena): Also please include the exact rollback steps in the runbook — we had trouble finding the rollback toggle during the incident.
10:29 Speaker 3 (Priya): We'll add explicit rollback steps and a test checklist.
10:36 Speaker 2 (Maria): Thank you everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.
10:40 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Thanks all, we'll follow up with the doc and schedule.
